question: What is the main job of the coronary circulation?

options.B: Supply oxygenated blood to the heart muscle
options.C: Filter waste products from systemic circulation
options.D: Pump blood directly to the lungs for gas exchange

explanation: Think of the heart as a hardworking engine—it pumps blood everywhere else, but it also needs its own private pipeline (the coronary vessels) to supply oxygen and nutrients so it can keep beating! [learn more](GNS111_U2_T10#GNS111_U2_T10_h1)

question: Why can't the heart muscle just use the blood sitting right inside its own chambers?

options.A: Endocardial lining blocks all nutrient absorption entirely
options.B: Intracardiac pressure destroys circulating red blood cells
options.C: Blood inside the chambers lacks adequate oxygen content
options.D: The chamber walls are too thick for simple diffusion

explanation: The heart walls are way too thick for nutrients to just soak through from the inside chambers. That's why the myocardium needs its own dedicated blood vessel network on the outside! [learn more](GNS111_U2_T10#GNS111_U2_T10_h1)

question: Where do the main coronary arteries start their journey?
explanation: The coronary arteries branch off right at the base of the aorta, where the blood pressure is highest and ready to rush into the heart muscle. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T10#GNS111_U2_T10_h2)

question: Which large vein collects used blood from the heart muscle and empties it into the right atrium?
explanation: The coronary sinus acts like a small drainage pipe that gathers up all the used, deoxygenated blood from the heart's veins and dumps it straight into the right atrium. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T10#GNS111_U2_T10_h2)

question: During which part of the heartbeat cycle does the heart muscle actually get most of its blood supply?
explanation: When the heart squeezes during systole, it pinches its own blood vessels shut! So, it mostly drinks up blood when it relaxes during diastole. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T10#GNS111_U2_T10_h3)

question: How does a dangerously fast heart rate (tachycardia) hurt the heart's blood supply?

options.A: It closes the aortic valve prematurely every cycle
options.B: It forces blood backward into the coronary sinus
options.C: It increases ventricular wall thickness permanently
options.D: It shortens diastole and reduces filling time

explanation: When the heart beats way too fast, it skips out on its resting time (diastole). Less rest means less time for blood to flow into the heart muscle! [learn more](GNS111_U2_T10#GNS111_U2_T10_h3)

question: What is the main thing that tells coronary blood vessels to open up wider when the heart works harder?
explanation: When the heart is working out or beating fast, it cries out for more oxygen. The blood vessels respond directly to this hardworking demand by opening up wider. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T10#GNS111_U2_T10_h4)

question: Which chemical messenger is released by heart cells during heavy work to widen blood vessels and bring more blood?
explanation: Adenosine is like a chemical flare released by stressed heart cells. It tells the local blood vessels to relax and widen so extra blood can rush in. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T10#GNS111_U2_T10_h4)

question: What is the medical term for chest pain caused by the heart muscle not getting enough blood?
explanation: Angina pectoris is that classic chest tightness or pain you hear about. It happens when the heart muscle is temporarily crying out for more oxygen. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T10#GNS111_U2_T10_h5)

question: What sudden event directly causes a heart attack (myocardial infarction)?

options.A: Gradual thinning of the left ventricular wall
options.B: Complete occlusion of a coronary artery by a clot
options.C: Temporary vasospasm during periods of mild rest
options.D: Inadequate venous return through the coronary sinus

explanation: A heart attack happens when a blood clot completely blocks a coronary artery, cutting off blood flow and causing that part of the heart muscle to suffer. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T10#GNS111_U2_T10_h5)

question: Which blood test is the gold standard for spotting injured heart muscle cells?
explanation: When heart muscle cells get damaged, they leak a protein called troponin into the blood. Finding this in a lab test is a clear sign of heart muscle injury. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T10#GNS111_U2_T10_h6)

question: A patient arrives complaining of sudden, crushing chest pain. What is your very first nursing action?

options.B: Schedule a routine lipid profile blood draw
options.C: Send the patient home with dietary brochures
options.D: Obtain a 12-lead ECG and assess vital signs

explanation: Chest pain is always an emergency! You need to check vital signs and run a 12-lead ECG right away to see what is happening to the heart. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T10#GNS111_U2_T10_h6)

question: How does a drug like nitroglycerin help a patient having an angina attack?

options.A: By increasing the heart rate to speed up circulation
options.B: By directly dissolving existing blood clots in vessels
options.C: By causing vasodilation to reduce myocardial workload
options.D: By thickening the blood to improve valve closure

explanation: Nitroglycerin relaxes and widens blood vessels. This makes it easier for blood to flow and lightens the load on the heart, easing that painful squeeze. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T10#GNS111_U2_T10_h7)

question: Which lifestyle change is most important for a patient recovering from a heart event?

options.A: Eliminating all fluid intake to reduce blood volume
options.B: Avoiding all forms of physical movement permanently
options.C: Complete strict bed rest for at least six months
options.D: Smoking cessation and heart-healthy diet adherence

explanation: Stopping smoking and eating heart-healthy foods tackle the root causes of blocked arteries, helping patients protect their hearts for the long run. [learn more](GNS111_U2_T10#GNS111_U2_T10_h7)
